1340:
Awe is a powerful feeling you get when you encounter something so grand, so vast, so beautiful, or so overwhelming that it seems far beyond ordinary experience. It stops you in your tracks. It makes you feel very, very small — and yet, strangely moved.

Think of standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon for the first time. The sheer size of it. The silence. The depth. The colors. You don't just think "oh, that's nice." Something much stronger happens inside you. You are almost unable to speak. You feel tiny. You feel like what you're seeing is somehow bigger than your mind can fully hold. That feeling is awe.
What Makes Awe Special — It's a Blend

Awe is not a single, clean emotion. It is a mixture of emotions happening at the same time:

  • Wonder — a sense that something is remarkable and amazing
  • Reverence — deep respect, as if the thing deserves to be honored
  • Humility — a feeling of your own smallness in the face of something greater
  • Sometimes, a touch of fear — not the fear of a spider or a dark alley, but the kind of fear that comes from encountering something vastly more powerful than yourself

These feelings hit you together, all at once, like a wave. That combination is what separates awe from lighter feelings like excitement or simple admiration.
The "Feeling Small" Element — The Heart of Awe

This is perhaps the most important thing to understand about awe: it makes you feel small.

But here is the key — it doesn't make you feel bad about being small. It's more like a sudden, humbling realization that the world is enormous and magnificent, and you are just one tiny part of it. It can even feel beautiful and comforting, like surrendering to something greater than yourself.

When a person stands under a sky full of stars and thinks, "There are billions of galaxies out there, and I am one person on one planet" — that dizzy, breathtaking, humbling sensation is awe.

Awe can be caused by many different things. Here are the main categories:

Nature:
The ocean in a storm. A towering mountain. A solar eclipse. Lightning splitting the sky. The silence of a vast desert. The northern lights rippling overhead. Nature, at its most grand and powerful, is one of the most common sources of awe.

Human achievement:
A great cathedral. A breathtaking piece of music that moves you to tears. A painting so skillful it looks almost alive. A speech so powerful it changes how you see the world. When humans create something that seems to go beyond ordinary human ability, it can produce awe.

Vastness and scale:
Anything that makes you suddenly aware of how enormous something is — the universe, deep time, the complexity of life — can produce awe. Looking at a photo of Earth from space and realizing how small your home planet looks is a classic example.

Great power:
A massive thunderstorm rolling across the sky. A roaring waterfall. A volcanic eruption seen from a safe distance. Witnessing enormous natural power can produce awe mixed with fear.

Spiritual and religious experience:
Many people feel awe in the presence of what they consider sacred — inside a grand place of worship, during a religious ceremony, or during a moment of deep prayer. This kind of awe has strong reverence at its center.

Extraordinary people:
Being in the presence of someone of exceptional talent, wisdom, or moral greatness — a brilliant scientist, a saintly figure, a legendary performer — can sometimes produce awe.
How Awe Feels — Physically and Emotionally

Awe has real physical signs. When people experience it:

  • They go quiet — words fail them
  • Their jaw may drop and their eyes widen
  • They may get goosebumps or feel a chill run through them
  • They feel frozen or rooted to the spot, unable to move
  • Their breath may catch in their throat
  • Time seems to slow down — they lose track of it entirely
  • Afterward, they often feel a sense of calm, peace, or being refreshed

Emotionally, awe often leaves a person feeling deeply affected — as if they have just witnessed something that matters, something important, something that will stay with them.
How Awe Differs from Similar Words

These words are related to awe but are not the same:

Wonder is lighter than awe. Wonder is curiosity and amazement — like a child watching a magician. It's delightful. Awe is heavier, deeper, and more humbling than wonder.

Amazement is mostly about surprise — something unexpected happened and you're stunned. Awe doesn't require surprise. You can plan a trip to the Grand Canyon, know exactly what it looks like from photos, and still be struck by awe when you actually see it.

Admiration is appreciation — you admire a skilled athlete or a smart person. Admiration doesn't require feeling small or overwhelmed. Awe does.

Reverence is deep respect, especially for something sacred or important. Awe can include reverence, but awe is more emotionally overwhelming. Reverence is quieter and more controlled.

Fear — in ordinary use, fear is about danger and threat. Awe can contain a flavor of fear, but awe is not fear. You can be in awe of something with no danger involved at all, like a beautiful sunset.
The Range of Awe — From Positive to Fearful

Awe sits on a spectrum:

On one end, awe is purely positive and beautiful — the awe of watching a stunning sunset, hearing a magnificent piece of music, or witnessing a kind and selfless act. This kind of awe feels uplifting and warm.

In the middle, awe is mixed — it contains both wonder and a certain kind of unease or emotional overwhelm. Standing at the edge of a cliff above a thousand-foot drop. Watching a ferocious storm at sea from the shore. You are moved, dazzled, and a little frightened at the same time.

At the other end, awe is fearful reverence — especially in older or religious language. Phrases like "the fear of God" don't mean being terrified of God the way you'd be terrified of a wild animal. They mean something closer to awe — a profound, humbling sense that God is infinitely greater and more powerful than you are, and that this demands your deepest respect.

In everyday modern usage, awe leans toward the positive and mixed middle, but it always carries that sense of being in the presence of something much greater than yourself.
Common Ways the Word Is Used

Awe almost always appears in these patterns:

  • "In awe" — the most common phrase. "She stood in awe of the painting." / "I was completely in awe."
  • "Filled with awe" — "He was filled with awe as the rocket lifted off."
  • "Struck with awe" or "struck dumb with awe" — meaning awe hit you so hard it left you speechless
  • "Stand in awe of" — "People stood in awe of her courage."
  • "Awe-inspiring" — an adjective describing something that produces awe. "The view was awe-inspiring."
  • "Awestruck" — an adjective for a person who has been hit by awe. "The tourists were awestruck."

Awe makes you feel small — but it also makes you feel connected. Connected to something greater. That's why awe, even when it includes a bit of fear, almost never feels purely negative. People seek awe. They travel across the world for it, they visit concert halls and national parks and places of worship for it. It feels meaningful and profound, like touching something real and important.

In short: awe is what you feel when you encounter something so magnificent, so vast, or so powerful that it momentarily takes you out of your ordinary self and reminds you that the world is far greater than you.
1341: Something that is awe-inspiring causes you to feel a powerful emotion called awe — a deep mix of wonder, amazement, and sometimes even a little fear, all at the same time. When something is awe-inspiring, it stops you in your tracks. It makes you feel small, yet lucky to witness it. It is something so grand, so powerful, or so extraordinary that your mind struggles to fully take it in.

To really understand this word, you need to feel what "awe" is, because the adjective is built entirely around that feeling.

Awe is not just being surprised. It is not just thinking "oh, that's nice" or "that's impressive." Awe is bigger than that. It is that feeling you get when you stand at the edge of the Grand Canyon and stare into its enormous depth. Or when you look up at a night sky full of stars in complete silence. Or when you watch a world-class musician perform something impossibly beautiful. Your jaw drops slightly. Your brain goes quiet. You feel both tiny and deeply moved at the same time. That feeling — that overwhelming, humbling, breathtaking sensation — is awe.

So, if something is awe-inspiring, it is the thing that produces that feeling in you.

Not everything impressive is awe-inspiring. A clean hotel room is nice. A well-cooked meal is impressive. But neither of these is awe-inspiring. The word carries a much heavier weight.

For something to be truly awe-inspiring, it usually has one or more of these qualities:

Enormous scale or power. Things that are vastly bigger, stronger, or more powerful than a human being tend to inspire awe. A thunderstorm at sea. A massive waterfall. A mountain range stretching to the horizon.

Exceptional rarity or perfection. Something so rare or so perfectly executed that it feels almost impossible — like a flawless athletic performance, or a piece of architecture that took centuries to build.

Deep beauty combined with emotional impact. It is not just pretty. It is the kind of beautiful that makes your chest feel tight and your eyes water.

Something that makes you feel your own smallness. This is a key part of awe. The universe is awe-inspiring partly because it reminds you how infinitely small you are within it.

Awe-inspiring is a strong adjective. It sits near the very top of the scale when you want to describe how impressive or moving something is. Here is a simple mental ladder to help you feel its position:

Okay → Good → Great → Impressive → Remarkable → Extraordinary → Awe-inspiring

Use it when "impressive" or "amazing" simply does not feel strong enough.

Here are examples that show you how the word feels in different situations:

  • "The view from the mountaintop was awe-inspiring — I could see four countries at once, and everything below looked like a map."
  • "Watching the rocket launch in person was an awe-inspiring experience. The noise alone shook the ground beneath our feet."
  • "She gave an awe-inspiring performance that left the entire audience completely silent for a moment before they burst into applause."
  • "The sheer size of the ancient temple was awe-inspiring. It was hard to believe human hands built something so enormous without modern machines."
  • "The surgeon's skill was awe-inspiring — he completed in two hours what most doctors would need six hours to do."

Notice that in every case, it is not just "big" or "good." There is a sense of being struck deeply, of feeling something powerful.
The Feeling It Puts on the Reader or Listener

When you use this word to describe something, you are not just saying it is large or beautiful. You are communicating that it triggers a specific emotional response — one of reverence, wonder, and a kind of respectful humility. This makes the word feel emotional and personal, not just factual.

It helps to know what this word should not be used for:

  • Do not use it for things that are merely good or pleasing. A tasty sandwich is not awe-inspiring.
  • Do not use it for things that are only surprising. A magic trick can be surprising without being awe-inspiring.
  • Do not use it so casually that it loses its power. If you call everything awe-inspiring, the word stops meaning anything. Save it for things that genuinely stop people in their tracks.

Breathtaking — very similar, but focuses more on beauty and visual impact. An awe-inspiring thing could be dark or frightening; a breathtaking thing is usually stunning in a pleasant way.

Magnificent — grand and splendid, but slightly more formal and less emotionally raw than awe-inspiring.

Majestic — suggests noble grandeur, often used for nature (majestic mountains, majestic eagles). Awe-inspiring has a slightly stronger emotional punch.

Staggering — emphasizes how hard something is to believe or comprehend, rather than the emotional wonder.

Humbling — captures the "feeling small" aspect of awe, but not the wonder and beauty side.

None of these synonyms fully replace "awe-inspiring." That combination of wonder + emotional overwhelm + a sense of your own smallness is unique to this word.

Awe-inspiring describes something so magnificent, powerful, or extraordinary that it produces a deep feeling of wonder and reverence in you — the kind that makes you feel small, speechless, and fortunate to witness it all at once.
1342: Awestruck means being completely overwhelmed by a feeling of deep wonder, admiration, and amazement — so much so that you are almost frozen, speechless, or stunned by it. When you are awestruck, something so grand, so powerful, so beautiful, or so extraordinary has entered your experience that your mind and body pause for a moment just to take it all in.
Understanding the Feeling from the Inside

To truly understand awestruck, you first need to understand awe — the emotion sitting at its heart.

Awe is not simple happiness, and it is not simple surprise. It is a rich, layered feeling made of several things happening at once:

  • A sense of wonder — your mind races, thinking "How is this even possible?"
  • A sense of deep admiration — you recognise that what you are seeing or experiencing is far beyond the ordinary
  • A sense of being humbled — you feel small, in a good way, because what you are facing is so much vaster or more powerful than yourself
  • Occasionally, a faint sense of reverence — almost like being in the presence of something sacred or untouchable

Now, the word "struck" in awestruck is doing important work. To be struck by something means to be hit by it — suddenly, powerfully, without warning. Think of being struck by lightning. You did not gradually walk into that feeling; it hit you. So awestruck tells you that awe did not creep in slowly — it arrived in a wave and overwhelmed you.

Put it together: awestruck = suddenly and completely overcome by awe.

The triggers for this feeling tend to be things that are vast, powerful, extraordinary, or deeply impressive — things that remind you how big and remarkable the world is. Common examples include:

  • Standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon and staring into its enormous depth
  • Watching a thunderstorm with lightning crashing across a wide open sky
  • Looking up at a sky full of stars on a clear night far from city lights
  • Watching an athlete do something that seems physically impossible
  • Hearing a musician perform with such breathtaking skill that the room goes silent
  • Seeing an ancient cathedral, a towering skyscraper, or a great work of art for the first time
  • Meeting someone of enormous talent or influence that you deeply admire
  • Learning a scientific fact — like the true size of the universe — that makes your mind stretch

Notice that these are not small, everyday things. Awestruck is reserved for moments of genuine magnitude.
The Emotional Texture: What Does It Feel Like?

When someone is awestruck, here is what is typically happening inside them:

  • Their breath catches — a brief, involuntary pause
  • They may go quiet or still — words feel suddenly inadequate
  • They feel a mix of joy and humility — thrilled by what they are seeing, but also aware of how small they are in comparison
  • There is often a feeling of being lucky to witness whatever is in front of them
  • Time may feel like it slows down for a moment

It is important to note that being awestruck is not the same as being scared, even though there is a slight edge of being overwhelmed. The feeling is almost always experienced as deeply positive — a gift, not a threat. However, if something is both spectacular and dangerous (like standing very close to a roaring volcano or a massive waterfall), the awe can carry a thin thread of fear woven into it. This is part of what makes awe a complex emotion.
How Intense Is It? (Placing It Among Similar Words)

It helps to understand awestruck by seeing where it sits on the scale of similar feelings:

Impressed → Amazed → Astonished → Astounded → Awestruck

  • Impressed is the mildest — "That was really good."
  • Amazed adds genuine surprise — "Wow, I didn't expect that at all."
  • Astonished is stronger — something shocking has stopped you in your tracks
  • Astounded is even more powerful — bordering on disbelief
  • Awestruck is at the deep end — it carries not just surprise, but wonder, admiration, and humility all at once. It is broader and more profound than simple shock.

A key distinction: you can be astonished by something small and unexpected (finding your lost keys in an odd place). You generally cannot be awestruck by something trivial. Awestruck requires something truly grand or magnificent.

Other words that are close but slightly different:

  • Spellbound — you are held completely captive by something, often by a story, a performance, or a personality; it emphasises being unable to look away more than deep humility
  • Dumbfounded — you are left speechless, but primarily from shock or confusion, not from wonder
  • Reverent — you feel deep respect, but it is calmer and more deliberate; awestruck is more sudden and overwhelming

These show you how awestruck is naturally used:

  • She stood awestruck at the edge of the waterfall, unable to speak.
  • The children were awestruck by the fireworks exploding above them.
  • He was completely awestruck when he finally saw the painting in person — photographs had not done it justice.
  • The crowd sat awestruck as the gymnast landed a move no one had ever seen before.
  • Tourists are often left awestruck when they first step inside the ancient temple.
  • Even after years of studying astronomy, she remained awestruck by the sheer scale of the universe.

Notice that in each sentence, the subject is passive — something happened to them. They did not decide to feel this way. It was brought upon them by the power of what they experienced.
Connotation: Is It Positive or Negative?

Awestruck is almost always positive or neutral. It describes a beautiful, elevating human experience. When someone is awestruck, it signals that they are capable of appreciating greatness — that they have not become so familiar with the world that nothing moves them anymore. In this sense, being called awestruck is never an insult.

It carries no negative connotation in normal use. It is not embarrassing to be awestruck; it is deeply human.
One Final Way to Lock It In

Imagine you are a person who has lived your entire life in a small, quiet village. One day, you travel for the first time and see the ocean — stretching out, vast and endless, further than your eyes can reach, with waves crashing with a sound like thunder. You have never seen anything like it. You stop walking. You forget to speak. Your chest feels full. You feel tiny and grateful all at once.

That is awestruck.
1343:
Awful means extremely bad, unpleasant, or of very poor quality. It describes something that makes you feel strongly negative — disgusted, unhappy, shocked, or horrified.

Think of it as a stronger version of the word "bad." If something is bad, it's not great. If something is awful, it's really, seriously bad — bad enough to affect your mood, your comfort, or your well-being.
What Kinds of Things Can Be "Awful"?

Awful is a very flexible word. It can describe almost anything that is bad in a strong way:

Physical things — things you experience with your senses:

  • "That milk has an awful smell." (it smells terrible)
  • "The food was awful." (it tasted really bad)
  • "The weather was awful today." (cold, stormy, miserable — really unpleasant)

Experiences and events:

  • "We had an awful time at the party." (the experience was terrible)
  • "It was an awful accident." (a very serious, distressing accident)
  • "The traffic was awful." (extremely bad, frustrating)

Quality of things:

  • "That was an awful movie." (very poorly made or very unenjoyable)
  • "His handwriting is awful." (very hard to read, very bad quality)
  • "The service at that hotel was awful." (very poor service)

Behaviour and character:

  • "She was awful to him." (she treated him very badly, cruelly)
  • "That was an awful thing to say." (it was unkind, hurtful, or very wrong)
  • "He's been an awful boss." (very difficult, unfair, or unpleasant to work with)

News and situations:

  • "I just heard the most awful news." (very sad or distressing news)
  • "They were in an awful situation." (a very difficult, serious, or troubling situation)

This expression deserves special attention because it has two different meanings depending on context:

  1. Physically sick: "I feel awful — I think I have a fever." Here, "awful" means you feel very unwell, like your body is suffering.
  2. Emotionally guilty or remorseful: "I feel awful about forgetting her birthday." Here, "awful" means you feel deeply sorry or ashamed. You're not sick in your body — you're troubled in your mind and heart.

The surrounding words (context) will always tell you which meaning is intended.

Sometimes, "awful" is used in a slightly different way — not to mean "bad," but simply to mean "very" or "a large amount of." In this use, it amplifies (strengthens) whatever word comes after it.

  • "There was an awful lot of work to do." → a very large amount of work
  • "She was in an awful hurry." → she was in a very great hurry
  • "It took an awful long time." → it took a very long time

This use is informal and common in everyday speech. Notice that in these sentences, "awful" is not calling anything bad — it's just saying that something exists in a very great degree. This is similar to how people use words like "terrible" ("a terrible lot") or "horrible" ("a horrible mess") in the same intensifying way.

There is one older, now largely outdated meaning of "awful" that you might come across in old books, religious writing, or very formal literary texts. In this older sense, "awful" meant inspiring deep awe, reverence, or wonder — something so powerful or grand that it fills you with a kind of fearful respect.

For example: "An awful silence fell over the cathedral." In this sentence, the silence is not described as bad — it is described as deeply solemn, almost supernatural in its weight, the kind of silence that makes you feel small.

You will rarely encounter this sense in modern everyday English. Almost every time you see or hear "awful" today, it means something bad. But it is good to know this older meaning exists so you are not confused if you ever come across it.

It helps to understand where "awful" sits on the scale of negative words:

Bad → Awful → Horrible / Terrible → Dreadful / Appalling → Atrocious

  • Bad is the general, mild negative word.
  • Awful is notably stronger — it suggests a real and strong negative impact.
  • Horrible / Terrible are roughly at the same level as awful, and the three are often interchangeable.
  • Dreadful is similar in strength to awful, but it often sounds more formal or old-fashioned.
  • Appalling / Atrocious are even stronger — these are used when something shocks or outrages you deeply.

So "awful" sits comfortably in the middle-to-strong range of negative adjectives. It's not a mild complaint, but it's also not the most extreme word in English for describing badness.

Since you're learning the adjective, it's worth knowing that the adverb form, "awfully," is commonly used — especially in British English — to mean "very" in a polite or warm way:

  • "That's awfully kind of you." (= that is very kind of you)
  • "I'm awfully sorry." (= I am very sorry)

In this adverb form, "awfully" has lost its negative meaning entirely and simply acts as a gentle intensifier. It can even sound quite charming or old-fashioned.

Core meaningExtremely bad, very unpleasant, of very poor quality
Can describeSmells, tastes, weather, experiences, events, quality, behaviour, news, feelings
"Feel awful"Either very physically unwell, or deeply guilty/remorseful
As intensifierSimply means "very" or "a lot" (awful lot, awful hurry)
Old meaningInspiring deep awe or reverence (rare in modern use)
StrengthStronger than "bad"; roughly equal to "terrible" and "horrible"

In short: if something is awful, it is bad in a way that is hard to ignore. It affects you — your senses, your mood, your comfort, or your moral sense. It is the word you reach for when "bad" simply does not feel strong enough.
1344: "Awkward" describes anything that doesn't fit smoothly or comfortably — a clumsy movement, an embarrassing social moment, a hard-to-handle object, an inconvenient time, or a person who doesn't quite know how to act. The feeling the word carries is one of something being slightly off, out of place, or not working the way it naturally should. Think of it as the opposite of smooth, easy, and natural.
1. Physically clumsy or ungraceful

When a person moves or performs an action without grace or coordination, we call it awkward. An awkward walk looks stiff or unbalanced. An awkward attempt to catch a ball looks clumsy and uncertain. An awkward wave goodbye might be a stiff, strange gesture that somehow doesn't look right.

The key idea is that the movement draws attention to itself precisely because it lacks the natural, smooth quality you'd expect. "He made an awkward jump and landed badly." "She gave an awkward smile — like she was forcing it."
2. Socially uncomfortable situations

This is probably the most common modern use. A situation, conversation, or moment is awkward when it makes the people involved feel uncomfortable, embarrassed, or unsure of what to say or do.

The classic "awkward silence" is when nobody speaks, and instead of feeling peaceful, it feels tense — like everyone is waiting for someone to say something but no one does. A first date with no chemistry is awkward. Running into an ex at a party is awkward. Saying something offensive by accident in front of a group and watching everyone go quiet — that's deeply awkward.

These situations feel awkward because of a mismatch: conversations are supposed to flow, social gatherings are supposed to have a comfortable energy, and when they don't, something feels wrong. "There was an awkward pause after she made the joke and nobody laughed." "He brought up money at the dinner table, and the whole room went silent. Very awkward."
3. Feeling awkward personally

A person can feel awkward as an internal emotion — meaning they feel self-conscious, out of place, or unsure of how to behave, even if nobody else around them feels the same way.

You might feel awkward at a formal party where you don't know anyone. You might feel awkward giving a speech if you're shy. You might feel awkward telling someone bad news. In each case, you feel uncertain and like you don't quite belong in the moment. "I always feel awkward when I have to speak in public." "She felt awkward being the only person who didn't know anyone."
4. A person who is socially awkward

When we describe someone as awkward — or "socially awkward" — we mean they generally struggle to handle social situations comfortably. They might say the wrong thing at the wrong time, not know when to stop talking, miss social cues, or simply seem uncomfortable around people.

It's worth knowing that being socially awkward is not inherently a flaw in character. Many people who are awkward are also kind, intelligent, and interesting. The word just describes the fact that social interaction doesn't come naturally to them. "He's a brilliant scientist but terribly awkward at parties." "She's a bit awkward at first, but once you get to know her, she's wonderful."
5. Difficult to use, handle, or move

An object can be awkward if it's hard to use or handle — usually because of its shape, size, weight, or position. This has nothing to do with emotions; it's purely about physical inconvenience.

"The sofa was an awkward shape and barely fit through the door." "Carrying three large bags at once is awkward." "The shelf is in an awkward spot — you keep hitting your head on it."

A task or problem can also be awkward when it's difficult to deal with — especially when there's no clean or easy solution. "Being asked to take sides in a fight between two close friends is an awkward position to be in."
6. Inconvenient timing

Something can be described as awkward if it happens at a time that is inconvenient or poorly chosen. "Could we reschedule? Three in the morning is an awkward time for a call." "You've caught me at an awkward moment — can I call you back in ten minutes?"
7. Being deliberately difficult (especially British English)

In British English particularly, if someone is "being awkward," it means they are deliberately uncooperative, stubborn, or obstructive — making things harder than they need to be on purpose. "Don't be awkward — just sign the form." "He's being awkward about returning the money."
The one big idea behind all the meanings

Look across all these uses and you'll notice one unifying thread: something that should flow or fit naturally doesn't. A movement lacks grace. A conversation lacks ease. An object lacks the right shape for the task. A time lacks convenience. A person lacks social comfort. In every case, "awkward" is pointing to that gap between how something should go and how it's actually going.
How it compares to similar words

Clumsy focuses specifically on lack of physical coordination — a clumsy person trips, drops things, and breaks things. "Awkward" is broader and covers social and situational difficulty too.

Embarrassing focuses on the emotion of embarrassment. An awkward moment is often embarrassing, but "awkward" also captures the tension of the situation itself, not just how someone feels about it.

Uncomfortable describes general discomfort. "Awkward" implies a more specific quality — the sense that something is out of place or doesn't fit, which is what causes the discomfort.

Inconvenient is the closest word to the "bad timing" sense of awkward, but "awkward" is softer and more conversational.
Common phrases to know

"An awkward silence" — a pause in conversation that feels tense rather than comfortable. "An awkward moment" — a brief, uncomfortable situation, usually social. "Put someone in an awkward position" — to place someone in a situation where any choice they make is difficult or uncomfortable. "Feel awkward" — to feel self-conscious or out of place. "A bit awkward" vs "terribly awkward" — you can use degree words freely with this adjective; the stronger the word, the worse the situation.
The related forms

Awkwardly (adverb): describes how something is done — "He laughed awkwardly." Awkwardness (noun): the state or quality of being awkward — "The awkwardness in the room was obvious."

In short, whenever you encounter "awkward," ask yourself: what is it that doesn't fit smoothly here? The answer will always point you to the right meaning.
1345:
Awkwardness is the quality or state of something — or someone, or a moment — being awkward. It means a lack of ease, grace, or smoothness. Whenever something doesn't flow naturally, feels uncomfortable, or is difficult to handle, that's awkwardness.

The word has three main senses, and all three share that same underlying idea: things not going as smoothly or comfortably as they should.

1. Social awkwardness — discomfort in a social situation

This is by far the most common use of the word today. Social awkwardness is that uneasy, self-conscious feeling that creeps in when a social interaction goes wrong, gets tense, or simply doesn't flow naturally.

Think about these moments: you wave back at someone who was actually waving at the person behind you. You forget someone's name seconds after being introduced. You make a joke and nobody laughs. You say "you too!" when a waiter says "enjoy your meal" — and then immediately wish you hadn't. The discomfort you feel in those moments, that squirming, wish-you-could-disappear sensation, is awkwardness.

Importantly, awkwardness can belong either to a person or to a situation. A person can have awkwardness as a personality trait — they struggle to interact smoothly with others, they don't read social cues well, they never quite know what to say. But a situation can also have awkwardness built into it — a tense silence, a reunion between two people who had a falling-out, a question nobody wanted to be asked out loud. In the second case, the situation itself is the source of the discomfort, not necessarily any single person.

2. Physical awkwardness — clumsiness, lack of grace in movement

This sense refers to moving or doing things in a way that is uncoordinated, clumsy, or ungraceful. A child just learning to write shows physical awkwardness in how they grip the pen. Someone just learning to dance shows it in their stiff, uncertain movements. Even a skilled person can experience physical awkwardness when doing something unfamiliar — like using chopsticks for the first time.

Physical awkwardness is essentially the opposite of being smooth, fluid, and confident in your body.

3. Situational awkwardness — something that is inconvenient or hard to deal with

This is the more practical, less emotional sense. Here, awkwardness simply describes a situation, arrangement, object, or timing that is inconvenient, poorly suited, or difficult to manage — not necessarily embarrassing, just tricky.

For example: "The awkwardness of the shape made the package nearly impossible to carry." Or: "There was an awkwardness in the timing of her resignation — it came right before the company's biggest project." The word here isn't about embarrassment at all. It just means something is not convenient or easy to work with.

When people refer to "the feeling of awkwardness," they almost always mean something specific: a mild but real emotional discomfort — a mix of embarrassment, self-consciousness, and not knowing quite what to do next. It's important to understand where awkwardness sits on the emotional scale.

It's milder than shame — shame is deep, painful, and cuts at your sense of who you are. Awkwardness is more surface-level. It stings a little, makes you wish you could rewind, but usually passes quickly and rarely leaves a lasting scar.

It's milder than fear — fear is about threat and danger. Awkwardness is about social discomfort and imperfection.

It's stronger than mere discomfort — awkwardness has that specific "out of place" quality, that feeling that something is off or wrong in the interaction.

Awkwardness can also exist between two or more people, almost like a fog that settles over a relationship or interaction. When two people haven't found their natural rhythm yet — maybe they've just met, or they've had a disagreement, or they share some kind of unspoken tension — there is awkwardness between them.

This relational awkwardness is different from hostility. It's not anger or hatred. It's a strained, uneasy quality where neither person quite knows how to be natural around the other. Think of running into an ex, or meeting a close friend's new partner for the first time when everyone is unsure how to act. That strained, uncertain atmosphere is awkwardness.

Awkwardness is a mild-to-moderate word. It doesn't describe a crisis. It's not a tragedy. Awkward moments are, almost by definition, temporary and survivable — they make for good stories later. The word carries a light, sometimes even humorous tone. People often laugh at awkwardness in hindsight, which is why so much comedy is built around it.

Depending on which sense you're using, awkwardness overlaps with several other words, though none of them are perfect replacements:

Clumsiness and ungainliness match the physical sense, but they say nothing about social discomfort.

Discomfort and unease capture the emotional feeling, but they're broader and don't carry that specific "things not flowing smoothly" quality that awkwardness has.

Inconvenience and difficulty match the situational sense, but they sound more practical and less expressive.

The true opposite of awkwardness — again depending on context — is grace, ease, fluency, or naturalness.

Awkwardness is the noun that names the quality of something lacking ease, grace, or smoothness. It can describe:

A social experience — the discomfort of an interaction that goes wrong or doesn't flow naturally. A physical quality — the clumsiness of movement or action in someone lacking coordination. A situational quality — the inconvenience or difficulty of something that is hard to manage or poorly timed.

Whenever something feels off — too tense, too clumsy, too uncomfortable, too inconvenient — the word that captures that quality is awkwardness.
1346: An awl is a small, simple hand tool designed to punch or pierce holes into materials. That's its one job — making holes. It does not drill, cut, or screw anything. It simply pushes through a material and creates a hole by forcing the material apart.

An awl has two parts:

  1. A handle — usually made of wood or plastic, shaped so your hand can grip it firmly, similar to the handle of a screwdriver.
  2. A metal spike — a sharp, pointed piece of steel sticking out from the handle. This spike is what does the actual work. It tapers to a very fine point, so it can push into materials easily.

Imagine a very thick, sturdy needle attached to a screwdriver handle — that mental image is essentially an awl.

You hold the handle, press the sharp point against the material you want to pierce, and then push (or twist while pushing). The spike forces its way through, displacing the material around it rather than removing any. The result is a clean, small hole.

This is different from a drill, which spins and removes material as shavings. An awl simply shoves the material aside to create a hole.

Awls are used wherever you need to make a precise hole in a firm or semi-firm material by hand:

  • Leather — This is the most common use. Shoemakers, belt-makers, and leather craftspeople use awls constantly to punch holes before sewing or inserting rivets. When you look at the holes in a leather belt where you fasten the buckle, those were made with an awl (or a similar tool).
  • Wood — Carpenters use a type of awl (called a bradawl) to make a small starter hole before driving in a screw or nail. This prevents the wood from splitting and gives the screw a precise starting point.
  • Fabric and canvas — Thick, heavy fabric like canvas can be pierced with an awl for sewing or attaching eyelets (the metal rings in tent tarpaulins, shoes, etc.).
  • Cork — Awls are sometimes used to pierce cork for various craft or practical purposes.
  • Marking/scribing — A type called a scratch awl is dragged across wood or metal to leave a thin, precise line as a guide for cutting or measuring.

While "awl" refers to the general category, there are a few named varieties based on use. You don't need to memorise these — just know they all belong to the same family:

  • Bradawl — a woodworking awl used to make pilot holes for screws.
  • Stitching awl (or sewing awl) — designed specifically for leather or thick fabric; the hole it makes is elongated (not round) so that a needle and thread can pass through.
  • Scratch awl — used mainly for marking and scribing lines on surfaces, not for making deep holes.
  • Cobbler's awl — used by shoemakers (cobblers) for piercing leather during shoe repair or construction.

• In a cobbler's shop (a shoemaker or shoe-repair shop)
  • In a leather goods workshop
  • In a carpenter's or woodworker's toolbox
  • In a camping or outdoor gear kit (for repairing tents, bags, straps)
  • In a general toolkit at home, often used for miscellaneous piercing tasks

• She used an awl to punch holes along the edge of the leather strap before sewing it together.
  • The carpenter pressed the awl into the wood to mark where the screw would go.
  • An awl is one of the oldest tools known to humans — simple, but incredibly useful.
  • He kept an awl in his toolkit for whenever he needed to make a quick hole in something tough.

An awl makes a hole — think of it as a "hole-maker." It's the most basic hole-punching tool you can hold in your hand. Whenever a craftsperson needs a precise, clean hole in leather, wood, or thick fabric and doesn't want to use a machine, they reach for an awl.
1347:
An awning is a roof-like cover — usually made of thick fabric or metal — that is attached to the outside wall of a building and sticks out over a window, a door, or an open area like a patio. Think of it as a small, permanent umbrella that is fixed to a building.

Its job is simple: block the sun, rain, or wind from reaching the space directly beneath it.

Picture a sloping, flat cover sticking out from the wall of a building. It is:

  • Attached at the top — fixed to the wall above a window or door.
  • Angled slightly downward toward the front, so rainwater can slide off.
  • Supported underneath by metal arms or brackets that hold it in place.
  • Usually wider than the window or door it covers.

If you have ever walked past a shop and noticed a colourful, striped shade sticking out above the entrance, that is an awning.

Awnings can be made from several materials:

  • Canvas or acrylic fabric — the most classic and common type. These are usually the ones you see in bright colours or stripes above shop doors.
  • Vinyl — a type of synthetic, waterproof plastic-like material.
  • Metal (aluminium) — for a harder, more permanent structure.
  • Polycarbonate — a clear or tinted hard plastic, used when you want light to pass through while still having protection.

An awning serves several practical functions:

  1. Sun protection — It blocks harsh sunlight from coming through windows or from beating down on you while you sit outside. This also keeps the interior of a building cooler.
  2. Rain protection — It lets you stand at a doorway or sit on a patio without getting wet when it rains.
  3. Wind shelter — It can reduce the force of wind in an outdoor seating area.
  4. Energy saving — By shading windows, awnings reduce the need for air conditioning inside a building.
  5. Appearance — Many shops use awnings to make their storefront look attractive and to display their shop name or logo.

Awnings appear in many different places:

  • Above shop or restaurant entrances — the most familiar use. A café, bakery, or clothing store will often have a fabric awning with the shop's name printed on it.
  • Above home windows and doors — to keep rooms cool and protect the entrance from rain.
  • Over patios and decks — a larger awning can cover an entire outdoor seating area of a home or restaurant, allowing people to sit outside comfortably.
  • On camper vans and RVs (caravans) — a special awning unfolds from the side of the vehicle to create a shaded outdoor space beside it.
  • On boats — a canvas awning is stretched over part of the deck to shade passengers.

This is an important distinction:

  • A fixed awning is permanently in place. It cannot be moved or folded. You will see these most often on shops.
  • A retractable awning can be rolled up or folded back when it is not needed — for example, on a sunny day when you want full sunlight on your patio, or when strong winds could damage it. These are common in homes and outdoor restaurant areas. They can be operated manually (by turning a handle) or automatically (with a motor and a remote control).
The Key Distinction — What an Awning Is NOT

It helps to know how an awning differs from similar things:

  • It is not a roof — a roof is a permanent part of a building's structure. An awning is an addition attached to the outside.
  • It is not a canopy — though these words are sometimes used loosely. A canopy is a similar covering, but it tends to be freestanding (supported by its own poles), whereas an awning is always attached to a wall or building.
  • It is not a tent — a tent is a fully enclosed portable shelter. An awning is open-sided and fixed to a structure.
  • It is not a blind or a curtain — those are inside a building. An awning is always on the outside.

These will help you see how the word is naturally used:

  • "The fruit seller pulled down the awning to protect his produce from the afternoon sun."
  • "We waited under the awning of the hotel while the taxi arrived in the pouring rain."
  • "The café had a red and white striped awning stretching out over the pavement."
  • "They installed a retractable awning over their patio so they could enjoy the garden even on hot summer days."
  • "Strong winds tore the awning clean off the front of the shop."
An awning is a fabric or metal cover fixed to the outside of a building that juts out like a sloping shelf above a window, door, or open area, providing shade and shelter from sun and rain.
1348:
AWOL stands for Absent Without Leave. When someone is described as AWOL, it means they have disappeared from a place where they were expected or required to be, without asking for or receiving permission to leave.

The word "leave" here doesn't mean "to leave a place." It means official permission to be away — like when an employee gets approved time off. So "without leave" = without permission.
Where It Comes From (Conceptually, Not Historically)

Think of it this way: imagine you have a responsibility — a duty, a job, a role — that requires you to be somewhere. Now imagine you simply vanish. No explanation. No approval. No warning. That is the heart of what AWOL means.
The Military Meaning (Its Strict, Original Use)

In its most precise and serious sense, AWOL is a military term. A soldier is AWOL when they leave their unit, post, or assigned location without getting official permission from a commanding officer.

This is not the same as being late, or taking a short break. An AWOL soldier has completely walked away from their duty — sometimes for hours, sometimes for days or even permanently — without authorization.

In the military, going AWOL is a punishable offense. It is treated seriously because a soldier's absence can directly affect the safety and effectiveness of their entire unit. The military distinguishes between being AWOL (absent for a limited, undefined time) and desertion (abandoning duty with no intention of ever returning), though in common speech, the two ideas are often blurred.

So when someone in the military is described as AWOL, it carries a strong sense of breach of duty — not just being absent, but being absent in a way that is unauthorized and irresponsible.

Over time, AWOL escaped the military and entered ordinary everyday language. Now it is widely used to describe any person (not just a soldier) who has gone missing from somewhere they were expected to be — without explanation or permission.

This informal use is very flexible. You can use it whenever someone has:

  • Vanished without notice
  • Stopped showing up
  • Become unreachable
  • Abandoned a role or responsibility unexpectedly

Examples:

  • "Our project manager has been AWOL all week — nobody can reach him."
  • "The team captain went AWOL right before the tournament."
  • "She's been AWOL from family dinners ever since she moved to the city."

In all of these cases, the person is absent, unaccountable, and without a valid or communicated reason. The word quietly signals that their absence is not okay — that someone or something is suffering because of it.
The Feeling and Tone the Word Carries

This is important: AWOL is not a neutral word. It carries a clear negative connotation. When you call someone AWOL, you are implying:

  • They had a responsibility to be somewhere or to someone.
  • They failed that responsibility.
  • Their absence was unexplained and unauthorized.
  • People are affected — left waiting, confused, or let down.

It is subtly accusatory. Saying someone is AWOL is stronger than simply saying they are "absent" or "missing." It frames their absence as a kind of abandonment — a failure of duty, whether that duty is a military post, a job, a team, or even a relationship.
A Key Distinction: AWOL vs. Just Being Absent

Not every absence is AWOL. If your coworker is sick and called in, they are absent — but not AWOL. If your friend is on vacation and told everyone in advance, they are away — but not AWOL. AWOL specifically requires two things working together:

  1. Absence — the person is not where they should be.
  2. No permission or explanation — no one approved it, and no one was told why.

Remove either of those two elements, and the word no longer applies.
Can It Apply to Things, Not Just People?

Yes, loosely. In informal speech, people sometimes use AWOL to describe things that have disappeared or are missing when they're needed:

  • "My motivation has gone completely AWOL this week."
  • "The instruction manual is AWOL — I can't find it anywhere."

This is a playful, metaphorical extension of the word, and perfectly acceptable in casual conversation.

AWOL describes someone (or something) that is missing from where they are supposed to be, without permission or explanation — carrying a clear implication that their absence is a failure of responsibility.
1349:
Awry means away from the correct, expected, or intended direction — either physically (something is crooked or twisted to one side) or, far more commonly, figuratively (something has deviated from how it was supposed to go).

Think of a straight path. You're walking on it perfectly. Then, without warning, something pushes you off it. That "going off the straight path" — that unexpected, unwanted deviation — is the soul of awry.

1. The physical sense (less common today)

In the literal, physical sense, awry describes something that is crooked, tilted, or twisted out of its proper position.

His tie hung awry around his neck.
The picture on the wall was hanging awry.

Both sentences mean the same kind of thing: the tie and the picture are not sitting straight — they're leaning or twisted to one side, off their correct position. If you straightened them, they would no longer be awry.

This sense is relatively rare in modern everyday language, but you will still encounter it in literature and formal writing.

2. The figurative sense (by far the most common)

This is the sense you will encounter almost all the time. Here, awry does not describe anything physically crooked. Instead, it describes plans, events, or situations that have gone wrong — specifically by deviating from what was intended or expected.

The key word here is deviate. Something awry isn't just bad — it started out fine (or was supposed to be fine) and then veered off course.

The plan went awry.
Everything went awry from the very first moment.
The rescue mission went awry when the helicopter broke down.

In all of these, there was an intention — a plan, an expectation — and something disrupted it, pulling it away from its intended course.
The phrase you will see most: "go awry"

The most natural and frequent way awry is used in English is in the phrase "go awry". If you remember nothing else, remember this phrase — it will serve you in almost every situation where this word is needed.

"Go awry" means: to not go as planned; to turn out badly or in the wrong direction.

More examples:

The wedding went awry when the caterer didn't show up.
The surgery went awry, and the patient needed emergency care.
Even the best-laid plans can go awry.

Notice that in every case, there was something that should have happened — a smooth wedding, a successful surgery, a plan working out — and it didn't. It went awry instead.
What makes "awry" different from just saying "wrong"?

You might be wondering: Why not just say "went wrong"? What does "awry" add?

Great question. While the two are often interchangeable, awry carries a slightly more specific and vivid picture. It subtly suggests a veering off course — like a ship that drifts from its charted route, or a bullet that deflects and misses its target. There is a sense of something that was on the right track, being pulled or pushed off it unexpectedly.

"Wrong" is broader and more neutral. "Awry" paints a more specific image of deviation. This is why awry is often preferred in formal, literary, or precise writing when the speaker wants to emphasize the idea of things straying from a proper course.

Awry can describe anything from a minor hiccup to a complete disaster — its severity is entirely decided by the context around it.

The picnic went slightly awry when it started to drizzle. (mild, almost humorous)
The entire mission went awry, costing many lives. (grave and serious)

The word itself is neutral in terms of intensity. You decide the weight by what surrounds it.
Register: when is this word used?

Awry sits comfortably in formal, semi-formal, and literary language. It is perfectly normal in everyday speech too, especially in the phrase "go awry," which is widely used across all registers. It is not slang, not outdated, and not overly technical — it is a solid, respectable English word that educated speakers use comfortably in both conversation and writing.

Awry is almost never placed before a noun. You would not say "an awry plan" or "the awry situation." Instead, it always comes after a verb.

✅ The plan went awry.
✅ Something is awry.
❌ The awry plan. (unnatural and incorrect)

This is what makes it an adverb — it describes how something goes (or is), not a noun directly.

What it meansAway from the correct or intended course; crooked (literally) or gone wrong (figuratively)
How to use itAlmost always after a verb: went awry, is awry, came awry
Most common form"Go awry" — meaning a plan or situation turned out badly
ToneNeutral to formal; works in everyday speech and writing
SeverityFlexible — can be mild or serious depending on context

To put it in the simplest possible sentence: if something goes awry, it means it has left the path it was supposed to stay on — and not in a good way.
